conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’m so glad you’re here.

Today I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week since your baby arrived. It’s not a test of your parenting—just a way to make sure we’re catching any bumps in the road early and getting you the right support.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or your baby’s safety. We’ll go at your pace, and if any question feels hard, we can pause or come back to it. When we finish, we’ll talk through what the results mean and what next steps might feel right for you.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

In the past seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent me that ridiculous video of cats knocking things over—but I’ve noticed it doesn’t come as easily. Most of the time I’m too tired or distracted by worrying about the baby to find much funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not so much, no. I mean, I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute meme, but it feels kind of forced. Mostly I’m just too worn out to feel any real spark of joy.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to look forward to little things—like my mom coming over tomorrow so I can shower without rushing—but the excitement feels pretty muted. I’ll think, “That’ll be nice,” but it lands flat, almost like I’m watching someone else’s life.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for almost an hour and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, maybe I’m not holding him right.” I know rationally it’s probably not my fault, but the thought still pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of times a day I’ll feel my heart start racing out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly worry the baby’s breathing sounds different, even though I just checked on him. It’s not constant, but it keeps catching me off guard.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened maybe twice this week. Once in the middle of the night when I was feeding him—everything was quiet, he was latched fine, but suddenly my chest got tight and I felt like I couldn’t catch my breath. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… especially by late afternoon. It feels like the dirty bottles, the laundry pile, and the texts I haven’t answered all gang up on me. I’ll think, “I should be able to handle this,” but some days it just feels like too much and I end up crying in the kitchen while the kettle boils.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll lie there after the baby finally dozes, running through “Did I sterilize the pump parts? Is he gaining enough weight?” That spiral keeps me up maybe three nights a week, but it’s worry, not straight sadness.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get waves of it, mostly in the evenings when the house is quiet. It’s not there all day, but I’ll suddenly feel this heavy sadness—like I’m missing something or I’m failing, even though I can’t put my finger on why. It usually passes if I distract myself with a show or scroll on my phone, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up a couple of times—once when my partner left for work and I felt alone—but actual crying? Maybe once this week, and it was over in a minute.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again.

You've shared that the sparkle of joy feels distant right now: jokes only bring a forced smile, and even small things like your mum's visit feel flat, as though you're watching life from the outside. Waves of <sym>sadness</sym> roll in most evenings, and worries about the baby race through your mind, making it hard to fall back to sleep. You're doing your best-getting out of bed, tending to every need-but you often blame yourself when your little one fusses and you end up <quote>crying in the kitchen while the kettle boils</quote>. You're exhausted, overwhelmed, and longing to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh and find joy, describing smiles as forced and limited to minor stimuli, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient can still anticipate small events but describes muted, flattened enjoyment that "lands flat," aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>The patient endorses self-blame "some of the time" ("a few times") with a recent, specific episode, matching the "Yes, some of the time" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unprompted anxious episodes occurring multiple times daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear episodes of sudden anxiety/panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness, shakiness) that came "for no very good reason," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Her vivid description of daily tasks "ganging up" and crying spells shows she is "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, identifiable waves of sadness that intrude multiple times per week, matching "Yes, quite often".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 16 places you well above the ≥14 threshold for <med>probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse loss of pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) and frequent <sym>low mood</sym> plus <sym>guilt cognitions</sym> that meet core <med>DSM-5 MDD criteria</medicine>. Additional <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> (sudden racing heart, breathlessness) are common in postpartum presentations and heighten distress. No self-harm thoughts means immediate safety, but functional impairment (sleep loss 3 nights/week, difficulty completing tasks) warrants prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or therapist trained in CBT or IPT for <med>postpartum depression</med>
3. Share Edinburgh results with your clinician so treatment options (therapy, medication, support groups) can be discussed promptly
4. Enlist help for night-time feeds once or twice a week to allow 4-5 hour stretches of sleep; practice wind-down routines (dim lights, no screens x30 min before bed)
5. Plan short daily outdoor walks with baby; daylight and gentle movement improve mood and sleep
6. Identify a trusted friend/family member to check in daily-brief calls/texts reduce isolation
7. Limit multitasking in late afternoon: set one small goal (e.g., fold one basket of laundry) and celebrate completing it
8. Keep tracking mood and anxiety in a phone note or calendar to review progress with your provider at follow-up
9. If low mood or panic spikes feel unmanageable before your appointment, call your local mental health crisis line or go to the nearest urgent-care centre
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening – 3 wk PP

Symptoms endorsed  
– Anhedonia: marked reduction in spontaneous joy and anticipatory pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
– Low mood: intermittent evening “waves” of sadness, tearfulness once/week (Q8, Q9)  
– Excessive guilt/blame over infant care (Q3)  
– Anxiety: episodic racing heart, nocturnal breathlessness/panic (Q4, Q5)  
– Overwhelm: daily late-afternoon distress, tearful when tasks accumulate (Q6)  
– Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worries about infant (Q7)

Patterns/Associated factors  
– Symptoms peak late afternoon/evening, improve with distraction  
– Insight intact; no self-harm ideation (Q10)

Risk indicators  
– Loss of pleasure, intermittent sadness, crying episode, guilt cognitions  
– Subsyndromal panic symptoms (twice/week)  
– Functional impact: difficulty completing household tasks, sleep loss 3 nights/week

Safety  
Denies any thoughts of self-harm; no current safety concern.

Screening impression  
Meets partial criteria for probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; further evaluation recommended to clarify severity and inform support plan.
